analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to fully disclose executive pay and lets large shareholders nominate corporate directors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its finance subcommittee until the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made executive pay a legitimate matter for shareholders to vote on. Public companies would have had to disclose, in plain dollar figures and charts, each director's and top executive's total pay — including stock options and deferred compensation counted at present value, and subtracted from reported earnings. Shareholders owning 3% of a company's voting stock or $1 million in shares could have placed their own director nominees on the company's official ballot, and companies would have had to hand over their shareholder lists to them, with fines for refusing.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders — including pension funds and ordinary investors whose retirement savings sit in these companies — gain the information and the power to challenge executive pay packages and elect directors. The Securities and Exchange Commission gains new enforcement tools, including fines for companies that refuse to provide shareholder lists.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a single total dollar figure for each director's and senior executive's compensation, including deferred, future, and contingent pay like stock options [S3].
Requires companies to estimate the present value of stock options and to subtract it from reported earnings, so profit figures reflect the true cost of executive pay [S3].
Declares executive compensation a proper subject for shareholder proposals, so companies can no longer omit those proposals from their proxy statements [S3].

Lets shareholders owning 3% of voting power or $1 million in market value nominate board candidates and have those nominations printed on the company's official proxy ballot, alongside management's picks [S3].
Requires companies to promptly provide their shareholder lists to investors entitled to them, with a monetary penalty from the SEC for failing to comply [S3].
Requires confidential proxy voting tabulated by an independent third party, reducing management's ability to know who voted against it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public companies and their executives and boards pay: pay packages become harder to obscure, reported earnings shrink by the cost of stock options, and boards face the first real possibility of challengers nominated by their own shareholders. Companies also bear new disclosure, list-production, and independent vote-tabulation costs.

drawbacks.text: The new disclosure, present-value calculations, shareholder-list production, and independently certified vote tabulation add compliance and paperwork costs to every covered public company, costs the subjects list itself flags as government paperwork [S3].

The $1 million market-value alternative to the 3% threshold lets any sizable investor or group — including activist funds with agendas unrelated to shareholder returns — nominate directors and use the company's own proxy materials to reach every shareholder [S3].
Counting stock options as an immediate earnings expense was, at the time, a change many companies argued would distort reported profits and discourage option-based pay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for ordinary investors are real but indirect: pay transparency and shareholder nomination rights matter most to pension funds and asset managers acting on savers' behalf, and the main costs are compliance expenses concentrated on corporate management. The design is relatively clean — disclosure with hard dollar figures and a genuine check on board entrenchment — though the low $1 million nomination threshold invites activist campaigns that may not serve average shareholders.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, passed to a finance subcommittee two weeks later, and nothing else ever happened to it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John W. Bryant (D-TX) introduced the Corporate Pay Responsibility Act on June 4, 1991 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
On June 17, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance — the last action of any kind in the bill's history [S5].
It had 2 Democratic cosponsors, and no committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate executives and boards came out ahead: nothing changed, so their pay stayed free of the new disclosure rules and their board seats faced no new shareholder-nominated challengers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; its sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, while the committee that buried it was chaired by a Democrat, leaving the partisan shape of the opposition unrecorded.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and boards of directors
industries.note: Their compensation would have had to appear as a single total dollar figure, with stock options expensed against earnings, and their pay policies would have become formally subject to shareholder votes. The bill's core transfer of power runs from management to the shareholders, including the pension funds that hold ordinary savers' money.

Companies would have faced new compliance costs — expanded disclosure, shareholder-list production, independently tabulated votes, and fines for noncompliance — against the benefit of cleaner governance. Management's interest in shielding pay decisions from shareholders sits against ordinary investors' interest in seeing and voting on them.

Funds and investors holding 3% of voting power or $1 million in shares would gain proxy access to nominate directors, mandatory shareholder lists, and confidential voting. Pension funds acting for working people were the natural users of these tools.
